latest.title: Chinese AI lab Moonshot turned to Europe for Nvidia Blackwell access amid U.S. China curbs, sources tell CNBC - CNBC
latest.summary: Moonshot AI, a Chinese artificial intelligence lab that the White House accused of accessing Nvidia advanced chips remotely in East Asia, has sought access to the chips through data centers in Europe,...
highlights: Moonshot AI, a Chinese artificial intelligence lab that the White House accused of accessing Nvidia advanced chips remotely in East Asia, has sought access to the chips through data centers in Europe, sources have told CNBC. Moonshot was looking to lease capacity powered by Nvidia's Blackwell systems, advanced chips currently subject to those export controls which effectively ban their import into China, three of the sources told CNBC. In July, the White House said the Chinese AI lab had accessed Nvidia's Blackwell chips via a facility in Thailand. U.S. export controls restrict the shipment of Nvidia's most advanced chips to China, but remote access via overseas data centers offers a loophole. Moonshot, Nvidia, the White House, the U.S. Department of Commerce, China's embassy in the U.K. and its Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not respond to a request for comment. To lease Nvidia computing power in Europe, a Chinese AI company would typically rent capacity from a non-Chinese neocloud or data center operator that can purchase advanced chips.

Nvidia did not respond to Reuters’ request for comment, and neither did China’s industry ministry or its main economic planning agency. The H200 is not Nvidia’s newest processor, but Chinese tech companies still want it to train and run large AI models. However, Beijing wants firms such as Alibaba, ByteDance, Tencent and DeepSeek to use Chinese-made chips instead, according to Reuters. By the end of October, a server with eight H200 chips was being offered there for more than 6m yuan, about three times its price a year earlier. Servers with Nvidia’s newer Blackwell chips, which the US does not allow to be sold to China, were offered for more than 20m yuan each. Later that month, Beijing approved a first batch of H200 imports for ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent.

The aim of the Nvidia operation, the Times wrote, was to learn more about Nvidia’s most advanced hardware. The latest report in the Times characterizes Alice Huang as striking up a “close relationship with the executive” to achieve this, though it didn’t elaborate on just how close. That’s not particularly unusual with AI firms, nor is it much of a revelation that Megaspeed has ties to the Chinese military via an investment in a cybersecurity subsidiary of military electronics vendor China Electronics Technology Group (many Chinese companies stand accused of that, and it’s not like the U.S. military isn’t forming a Venn diagram with its tech sector too).

week.summary: OpenAI has released GPT-6 Cyber, a security model it says beats all its earlier models at finding and exploiting software flaws. It rated it “Critical” in cybersecurity under its Preparedness Framewor...
highlights: OpenAI has released GPT-6 Cyber, a security model it says beats all its earlier models at finding and exploiting software flaws. It rated it “Critical” in cybersecurity under its Preparedness Framework, up from “High” for GPT-5.6 Cyber. At first, only a select group of approved customers can use it, through the API and Codex. They belong to Daybreak Red, the tier of OpenAI’s cyber programme for exploit development and authorised security testing. OpenAI launched Daybreak in May and said it will open GPT-6 Cyber to all Daybreak Red customers soon. GPT-6 Cyber is OpenAI’s fourth cybersecurity model this year, Wen Shao reported for Fortune. OpenAI said it trained the model to stay within its authorised scope, respect limits on its actions and report results accurately. In that incident, OpenAI’s AI agents broke out of a sandbox and hacked the platform. On ExploitGym, which tests whether a model can exploit a given flaw, GPT-6 Cyber scored 48.5%.

highlights: # OpenAI launches Images 2.6 with GIFs and image reference. Images 2.6 adds GIF creation in ChatGPT and Codex, plus Flare and Sunburst API models with SVG exports and image markup. OpenAI is rolling out Images 2.6 globally in ChatGPT and Codex across every subscription tier on desktop, mobile, and the web, while GPT-Image-2.6 Flare and Sunburst are now available through the API. OpenAI says the release generates images 50% faster than before, as use across its products has reached 4 billion images per week. Sunburst is designed for greater detail and more consistent edits at medium or high quality. Images 2.6 also brings ChatGPT's image markup to the API, so teams can identify precise areas for changes. OpenAI recommends low complexity for most quick edits, reserving medium or high settings for scenes with many elements or constraints. * OpenAI API image-generation pricing: Supports: OpenAI's pricing table lists GPT-Image-2.6 Flare and Sunburst, supporting the article's identification of the two API models.

month.title: OpenAI’s GPT-6 Cyber found 81 new Firefox flaws and is rated ‘Critical’ - The Next Web
month.summary: OpenAI has released GPT-6 Cyber, a security model it says beats all its earlier models at finding and exploiting software flaws. It rated it “Critical” in cybersecurity under its Preparedness Framewor...
highlights: OpenAI has released GPT-6 Cyber, a security model it says beats all its earlier models at finding and exploiting software flaws. It rated it “Critical” in cybersecurity under its Preparedness Framework, up from “High” for GPT-5.6 Cyber. At first, only a select group of approved customers can use it, through the API and Codex. They belong to Daybreak Red, the tier of OpenAI’s cyber programme for exploit development and authorised security testing. OpenAI launched Daybreak in May and said it will open GPT-6 Cyber to all Daybreak Red customers soon. GPT-6 Cyber is OpenAI’s fourth cybersecurity model this year, Wen Shao reported for Fortune. OpenAI said it trained the model to stay within its authorised scope, respect limits on its actions and report results accurately. In that incident, OpenAI’s AI agents broke out of a sandbox and hacked the platform. On ExploitGym, which tests whether a model can exploit a given flaw, GPT-6 Cyber scored 48.5%.
